spec.topic: Should national elections use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: National elections should use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies. The reason is that under the current system millions of votes cast for losing candidates have no effect on who sits in parliament.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: That matters beyond fairness, since voters who see their ballots count for nothing are more likely to stay at home next time.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Proportional systems do tend to produce coalition governments.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say coalitions are unstable and indecisive, so proportional representation would weaken government.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But that ignores how coalitions force parties to negotiate, and that bargaining is often what keeps policy moderate and durable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once lived in a safe seat where the same party won by thirty points for decades.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, proportional representation would make every vote matter to the final result, which is the fairest way to translate votes into seats.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Incidentally, ballot papers in my town are still counted by hand.

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether criminal trials for every serious offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, begin with you.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: A single juror can block a verdict under a unanimous-jury rule. Because that one-person veto can leave a case unresolved, unanimity makes hung trials more likely.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Unanimity gives every juror an equal voice. That safeguard matters especially when the charge carries a severe sentence.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, does the possibility of a hung trial outweigh that safeguard?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Several legal systems permit qualified-majority jury verdicts. Since those systems recognize such verdicts, a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Jury deliberations often expose weaknesses in the evidence. That is why requiring unanimity would improve the accuracy of serious-offence verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what is the practical cost when a jury cannot agree?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Hung trials force victims to endure another legal proceeding. Because avoiding unnecessary retrials is valuable, that is a reason not to demand unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has now raised fairness, accuracy, and the burden of retrials. Yara, where do you stand?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: I am concerned that a narrow majority could convict someone despite serious doubts. The courthouse in my district has two jury rooms.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I once served on a jury. Majority verdicts can reflect careful jury deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: For that reason, serious offences should not require unanimous jury verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: But that conclusion is mistaken: serious offences deserve the strongest protection against wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's point is that unanimity gives every juror an equal voice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Chidi's position is that a qualified-majority jury verdict can still be lawful.

utterances.text: National elections should use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies. The reason is that under the present system millions of votes go to losing candidates and so have no effect on who sits in parliament.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say that proportional systems tend to produce coalition governments that are unstable and slow to act.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But several countries with proportional representation have had coalitions that lasted a full term and passed major reforms.

utterances.text: Proportional representation would give small parties a fair share of seats.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, a parliament in which each party's seats match its share of the votes is more legitimate in the eyes of voters, which is one more reason to switch.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once lived in a town where the same party held the seat for forty years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Proportional lists would also require parties to publish their candidate rankings before the election.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Should planning rules require every new home to include a rainwater-collection system?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, planning rules should require every new home to include one. Many regions face increasingly frequent water shortages, which is one reason for that requirement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What practical benefit would the systems provide?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater-collection systems reduce a home's demand for treated mains water. The average roof area in the proposed development is 118 square metres.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would a mandate also help the construction industry?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes. A national requirement would create a predictable market for rainwater-system installers, which is another reason to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Critics say one rule cannot suit every climate.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A single national requirement would be unfair in regions with very low rainfall. Even so, collected rainwater is useful for garden watering and laundry, so the rule has clear everyday value.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you support requiring rainwater systems in all new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Exactly; planning rules should require rainwater systems in all new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Would the collected water be safe to drink?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater systems should supply only non-potable household uses. Using collected rainwater for toilet flushing can substantially reduce treated-water consumption.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So you are saying the systems would serve garden watering, laundry, and toilet flushing rather than drinking-water taps?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: That is right. Installing collection systems during construction is cheaper than adding them to completed homes, which is a strong reason to regulate them at the planning stage.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Several older homes in my street have recently replaced their front doors.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: Apart from cost, can the systems work reliably?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Rainwater tanks can provide water for toilet flushing during ordinary dry spells. Modular rainwater tanks are straightforward for building inspectors to check.

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: A rule can require an overflow outlet that directs excess water safely away from foundations; that is a further reason for setting a common standard. Most new homes already have gutters that can feed a collection tank, so the requirement would usually be easy to implement.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: In other words, Gwen supports a universal rainwater-system requirement for new homes?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Yes, provided the systems are designed for non-potable uses and include safe overflow arrangements.
